screens.title: Custom Exceptions and try-with-resources
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why defining your own exception types improves clarity and how Java’s try-with-resources automatically closes resources for you. We begin by motivating custom exceptions: when a built-in exception like IllegalArgumentException or RuntimeException is too generic, a domain-specific class such as InsufficientFundsException or ProductNotFoundException communicates intent immediately. You will see how to choose checked versus unchecked: checked when callers can recover, unchecked when the error indicates a programming or configuration problem. Next we introduce try-with-resources and the AutoCloseable contract, showing how resources declared in the try statement are closed automatically and how multiple resources are closed in reverse order. We’ll also cover suppressed exceptions: when an exception thrown during close is attached to a primary exception so you don’t lose the original failure. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to implement both custom exceptions and safe resource handling, wrap lower-level input and output failures in higher-level exceptions, and reason about suppression when debugging. Ready to make your error handling clearer and safer?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Overview

Custom Exceptions & try-with-resources

Design domain-specific errors and use language support to manage resources cleanly.

In this lesson
When and how to write custom checked and unchecked exceptions.
Coming up
AutoCloseable, try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions.
Hands-on
Build a FileProcessor that wraps I/O errors in FileProcessingException.
Explore Key Topics
Custom Exception

Define a checked or unchecked class to make errors expressive in your domain code.

try-with-resources

Declare AutoCloseable resources in the try header for guaranteed close and simpler code.

Suppressed Exceptions

The primary exception remains visible while close-time failures are attached as suppressed exceptions.

Quick Visual
Domain-specific exceptions communicate intent.
Resources declared in the try are closed automatically.
Why start here

Clear errors and automatic resource management reduce bugs and improve maintainability. This chapter gives tools you will use in real Java applications to make failure modes explicit and safe.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives give you a clear map for what we will practice and why it matters. First, you'll design and implement custom checked and unchecked exceptions so your code reports problems in terms your domain understands. For example, a banking application benefits from an InsufficientFundsException that carries amounts so callers can react intelligently. Second, you'll learn to decide when a custom exception is appropriate versus using a built-in class: use checked exceptions when callers can recover, unchecked when the problem indicates a bug or misconfiguration. Third, you'll use try-with-resources to ensure streams and other AutoCloseable resources are closed reliably with far less boilerplate than a manual finally block. Fourth, you'll understand suppressed exceptions so you can inspect any errors raised during resource cleanup without losing the primary cause. Each objective includes a small competency milestone so you can confirm you integrated these practices into real code. These skills reduce hidden resource leaks, clarify error handling, and make debugging more efficient.

screens.title: Why create custom exceptions?
screens.narratorSegment: Custom exceptions make your program's failure modes explicit. A well-named exception communicates a business condition directly, reducing the need for comments or ad-hoc string parsing. For example, a banking method that throws InsufficientFundsException gives callers immediate information about the cause and often includes fields such as requiredAmount and availableBalance so client code can react, present messages, or log structured data. Custom exceptions also enable more precise catch blocks. Instead of catching a generic Exception or RuntimeException and risking swallowing unrelated problems, you can catch the specific class and handle it appropriately. A common misconception is that custom exceptions add unnecessary classes; instead they act as lightweight contract elements describing what can go wrong. Another trap is overuse: don't create an exception for every minor check. Prefer checked exceptions for recoverable conditions where callers should explicitly handle the situation, and prefer unchecked exceptions when the problem indicates a bug or misconfiguration. The core takeaway: custom exceptions improve readability and handling when used to model meaningful domain failures. Why create custom exceptions? means a custom exception is a user-defined class extending exception or runtimeexception to represent domain-specific failure.. In practical terms, express domain errors with precise types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Why create custom exceptions?
Definition

Custom Exception

A user-defined class that models domain errors and carries context so callers can make informed decisions.

When to use
Model recoverable domain failures or clearly named error conditions that callers should handle.
Avoid
Do not create trivial exceptions for every boolean check; prefer existing exceptions when they convey intent sufficiently.
Key Takeaway

Use custom exceptions to encode domain intent and pass structured error details to callers.

Concrete Example
InsufficientFundsException (concept)
class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
  private double requiredAmount;
  private double availableBalance;

  public InsufficientFundsException(String message, double required, double available) {
    super(message);
    this.requiredAmount = required;
    this.availableBalance = available;
  }

  public double getRequiredAmount() { return requiredAmount; }
  public double getAvailableBalance() { return availableBalance; }
}
Analogy
Think of a custom exception as a labeled container for failure details, like a form that contains the exact fields needed to resolve the issue.

screens.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing checked or unchecked for a custom exception is a design decision about who must do the work of recovery. Checked exceptions extend Exception and force callers to declare or catch them. Use checked exceptions when the caller can reasonably recover — for instance, an InvalidCredentialsException might be checked so calling code must handle prompting the user. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are used when the error indicates a programming mistake or unrecoverable configuration issue; callers are not forced to handle them. A common misconception is that checked exceptions are obsolete; rather, they are tools for A P I design when recoverability is expected. Another trap is overusing checked exceptions for every failure, which leads to noisy code. The practical rule from this chapter is simple: prefer checked for recoverable domain conditions, and prefer unchecked for developer errors or unexpected states. This distinction influences method signatures and how client code handles failure paths. Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions means use checked exceptions for recoverable domain conditions; use unchecked for programming or configuration errors.. In practical terms, how to choose between exception and runtimeexception. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Checked vs Unchecked
Checked
Extend java.lang.Exception
  • Compiler forces callers to catch or declare the exception.
  • Use when the caller can handle or recover from the condition.
  • Makes the API contract explicit in method signatures.
Example use
Authentication failure that requires user action is a good candidate for a checked exception.
Unchecked
Extend java.lang.RuntimeException
  • Callers are not forced to handle the exception.
  • Use for programming errors or unrecoverable configuration problems.
  • Avoid using unchecked for recoverable domain conditions.
Example use
Missing application configuration that prevents startup may be modeled as an unchecked exception.
Common mistake
Converting every failure to unchecked hides recovery opportunities and shifts responsibility away from callers who should handle certain errors.
Pro tip
If in doubt, prefer checked for user-facing recoveries and unchecked for developer faults.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › InsufficientFundsException
Exception Code
class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {
  private double requiredAmount;
  private double availableBalance;

  public InsufficientFundsException(String message, double requiredAmount, double availableBalance) {
    super(message);
    this.requiredAmount = requiredAmount;
    this.availableBalance = availableBalance;
  }

  public double getRequiredAmount() { return requiredAmount; }
  public double getAvailableBalance() { return availableBalance; }
}
Usage
public void withdraw(double amount) throws InsufficientFundsException {
  if (amount <= 0) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Withdrawal amount must be positive.");
  }
  if (balance < amount) {
    throw new InsufficientFundsException(
      "Cannot withdraw " + amount + ". Insufficient funds.", amount, balance);
  }
  balance -= amount;
}
Handler
Catch InsufficientFundsException and use getters to decide whether to prompt, retry, or suggest a transfer.

screens.title: Using custom unchecked exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Custom unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are useful for configuration or programming errors that callers cannot reasonably handle. The chapter shows InvalidConfigurationException as an example: it signals missing application configuration and can optionally wrap a cause. Unlike checked exceptions, callers are not obliged to catch unchecked exceptions, which makes them appropriate for startup-time problems where there is no useful recovery path. In practice, reserve unchecked exceptions for situations where the program cannot continue or where handling would be scattered and unreliable. One misconception is to use unchecked exceptions purely to avoid changing method signatures; that hides the contract. If you expect callers to act, prefer checked. The example usage includes checking a system property and throwing InvalidConfigurationException when the property is absent and catches it only to report the configuration issue. This pattern keeps validation logic expressive while leaving runtime control flow clear. Using custom unchecked exceptions means invalidconfigurationexception models unrecoverable setup problems and can optionally include a cause to aid debugging.. In practical terms, when runtimeexception is appropriate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Unchecked Exceptions
Exception Code
class InvalidConfigurationException extends RuntimeException {
  public InvalidConfigurationException(String message) {
    super(message);
  }
  public InvalidConfigurationException(String message, Throwable cause) {
    super(message, cause);
  }
}
Usage Pattern
Check configuration at startup. If required settings are missing throw InvalidConfigurationException. Catch it at a high level to report and stop initialization.
Misconception
Using unchecked exceptions only to avoid signature changes sacrifices API clarity. Choose them for genuine non-recoverable faults.

screens.title: try-with-resources: automatic closing
screens.narratorSegment: try-with-resources replaces verbose finally blocks with a concise declaration that guarantees close is invoked. The pattern is simple: declare one or more resources that implement AutoCloseable in the try header. When the try block finishes, the runtime calls close() on each resource in reverse order of declaration. This behavior means resources are reliably released whether the try exits normally or by throwing an exception. A common mistake is assuming try-with-resources swallows exceptions; it does not. Exceptions from the try block still propagate to your catch, and any exceptions thrown during close are attached as suppressed exceptions to help debugging. Another trap is attempting to use types that do not implement AutoCloseable; the code will not compile. Benefits include less boilerplate, fewer null checks in finally blocks, and clearer intent. Use try-with-resources whenever you work with streams, readers, sockets, or any custom resource implementing AutoCloseable. try-with-resources: automatic closing means declare autocloseable resources in the try header; they are closed automatically in reverse order when the block exits.. In practical terms, how try-with-resources simplifies cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › try-with-resources
Pattern
Declare resources in the try header. When the try block ends, each resource's close() is called automatically.
1
Open resource
2
Use resource
3
Automatic close (reverse order)
Important
try-with-resources guarantees close is invoked even when exceptions occur, but you still need catch blocks to handle read-time or close-time exceptions.
Quick Example
try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(filePath))) {
  String line;
  while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) {
    System.out.println(line);
  }
} catch (IOException e) {
  System.err.println("Error reading or closing file (TWR): " + e.getMessage());
}

screens.title: Try-with-resources: multiple resources and closing order
screens.narratorSegment: When you declare multiple resources in a single try-with-resources, Java closes them in reverse order. This is important when resources depend on each other, such as a FileReader wrapped by a BufferedReader. Closing the wrapper first prevents it from trying to use the underlying stream after it is closed. The code example declares FileReader first and BufferedReader second; on exit, BufferedReader. close runs before FileReader. close. This reverse closing order ensures nested wrappers are released safely. It also matters for suppressed exceptions: if the try block throws and a later close throws too, the close exceptions are suppressed and attached to the primary exception. A common mistake is assuming declaration order implies close order; it does not. Another practical benefit is that you can declare local resources that implement AutoCloseable inline in the try header, reducing the need for temporary variables and null checks in finally blocks. Keep dependencies in mind when ordering resources. Try-with-resources: multiple resources and closing order means multiple resources are closed in reverse order of declaration — wrappers should be declared after the resources they wrap so they close first.. In practical terms, why resources are closed in reverse of declaration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Multiple Resources
Example
try (FileReader fr = new FileReader(filePath);
     BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(fr)) {
  String line;
  while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) {
    System.out.println(line);
  }
} catch (IOException e) {
  System.err.println("Error with multiple resources: " + e.getMessage());
}
Why reverse order
The wrapper (BufferedReader) depends on the underlying FileReader. Closing the wrapper first avoids using a closed underlying resource and prevents subtle I/O errors.
Quick Tips
  • Declare wrappers after their underlying resources.
  • Expect close() to run even on exceptions.
  • Inspect suppressed exceptions to see close-time failures.

screens.title: AutoCloseable and Closeable
screens.narratorSegment: AutoCloseable defines a single method, close(), which may throw Exception. Any class implementing AutoCloseable can be declared in a try-with-resources header and will be closed automatically when the block exits. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › AutoCloseable
AutoCloseable
Defines void close() throws Exception. Implementing it enables try-with-resources support.
Implementation notes
  • Make close() idempotent when possible.
  • Release native handles and free buffers inside close().
  • Decide whether close() should throw an exception to signal cleanup failure.
Closeable
Extends AutoCloseable and declares close() throws IOException. Most I/O classes implement Closeable.
Starter ResourceReader
class ResourceReader implements AutoCloseable {
  private boolean closed = false; 
  private int readCount = 0;

  public String readLine() throws IOException { ... }

  @Override
  public void close() throws IOException {
    System.out.println("ResourceReader 'Name' closing...");
    this.closed = true;
  }
}

screens.title: Suppressed Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Suppressed exceptions occur when an exception thrown in the try block is followed by another exception thrown during automatic resource close. Java treats the first exception as primary and adds the later close-time exceptions to it as suppressed. This preserves the original failure context while making additional issues available via Throwable. getSuppressed(). The chapter includes a FileWriter example where a write throws an IOException and close also throws another IOException; the catch block receives the write exception and can inspect suppressed exceptions to see the close-time message. A typical debugging approach is to log the primary exception and iterate over getSuppressed() to capture any secondary issues. A misconception is that suppressed exceptions are hidden; they are accessible but require explicit inspection. Use suppressed exceptions to understand cleanup failures without losing the original error that likely caused the failure in the first place. Suppressed Exceptions means when close() throws after a primary exception, the close-time exception is added to the primary one and available via getsuppressed().. In practical terms, preserving primary causes when close() fails. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are predictable mistakes developers make when working with custom exceptions and try-with-resources. First, overusing custom exceptions for trivial checks clutters an A P I and creates maintenance overhead. Ask if a built-in exception already expresses the problem. Second, converting recoverable failures to unchecked exceptions hides the need for callers to handle foreseeable conditions. Third, failing to implement close() as idempotent can cause repeated cleanup logic to misbehave under multiple close calls. Fourth, not inspecting suppressed exceptions can hide important close-time failures; always check getSuppressed when debugging resource-related errors. Fifth, attempting to use try-with-resources with non-AutoCloseable types fails at compile time. Best practices: model failures at the level of the A P I consumer, provide constructors that accept a cause when wrapping lower-level exceptions, order resources so wrappers close first, and write clear catch blocks that both handle the primary exception and log suppressed entries for diagnostics. These habits make your code safer and easier to operate. Common pitfalls and best practices means avoid unnecessary exceptions, misuse of unchecked exceptions, and ignoring suppressed exceptions; implement close() carefully and order resources correctly.. In practical terms, avoid misuse while designing exceptions and resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the three core concepts to remember. First, a Custom Exception is a user-defined class extending Exception or RuntimeException to represent domain-specific errors. It carries structured details that enable programmatic handling and clearer logs. Second, try-with-resources is a Java 7+ statement that automatically closes AutoCloseable resources declared in the try header, reducing boilerplate and preventing resource leaks. Third, suppressed exceptions happen when a close() throws after a try-block exception; the primary exception is propagated and close-time exceptions are attached and retrievable via getSuppressed(), which is important for thorough debugging. Keep these concepts in mind: model failures at the appropriate level, use try-with-resources whenever possible, and inspect suppressed exceptions when cleanup problems occur. These practices improve code clarity, prevent leaks, and make production failures easier to diagnose. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why defining your own exception types improves clarity and how Java’s try-with-resources automatically closes resources for you. We begin by motivating custom exceptions: when a built-in exception like IllegalArgumentException or RuntimeException is too generic, a domain-specific class such as InsufficientFundsException or ProductNotFoundException communicates intent immediately. You will see how to choose checked versus unchecked: checked when callers can recover, unchecked when the error indicates a programming or configuration problem. Next we introduce try-with-resources and the AutoCloseable contract, showing how resources declared in the try statement are closed automatically and how multiple resources are closed in reverse order. We’ll also cover suppressed exceptions: when an exception thrown during close is attached to a primary exception so you don’t lose the original failure. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to implement both custom exceptions and safe resource handling, wrap lower-level input and output failures in higher-level exceptions, and reason about suppression when debugging. Ready to make your error handling clearer and safer?

These learning objectives give you a clear map for what we will practice and why it matters. First, you'll design and implement custom checked and unchecked exceptions so your code reports problems in terms your domain understands. For example, a banking application benefits from an InsufficientFundsException that carries amounts so callers can react intelligently. Second, you'll learn to decide when a custom exception is appropriate versus using a built-in class: use checked exceptions when callers can recover, unchecked when the problem indicates a bug or misconfiguration. Third, you'll use try-with-resources to ensure streams and other AutoCloseable resources are closed reliably with far less boilerplate than a manual finally block. Fourth, you'll understand suppressed exceptions so you can inspect any errors raised during resource cleanup without losing the primary cause. Each objective includes a small competency milestone so you can confirm you integrated these practices into real code. These skills reduce hidden resource leaks, clarify error handling, and make debugging more efficient.

This second objectives screen focuses on concrete tasks and how to show competency. You will implement a checked FileProcessingException that accepts an optional cause so you can wrap lower-level input and output failures. You will also implement ResourceReader that implements AutoCloseable; its readLine method simulates limited reads and throws IOException when exhausted. Using try-with-resources, you will open a ResourceReader and allow automatic closing to run even when an exception is thrown. The activity requires catching FileProcessingException in main and printing details including the cause stack trace if present. These tasks reinforce practical patterns: wrap technical exceptions in domain exceptions for clearer error reporting, implement AutoCloseable properly so resources close reliably, and inspect suppressed exceptions to find closing-time failures. Completing these milestones ensures you can both design exceptions and use language features to prevent resource leaks. That combination leads to code that is safer to run and easier to debug.

Custom exceptions make your program's failure modes explicit. A well-named exception communicates a business condition directly, reducing the need for comments or ad-hoc string parsing. For example, a banking method that throws InsufficientFundsException gives callers immediate information about the cause and often includes fields such as requiredAmount and availableBalance so client code can react, present messages, or log structured data. Custom exceptions also enable more precise catch blocks. Instead of catching a generic Exception or RuntimeException and risking swallowing unrelated problems, you can catch the specific class and handle it appropriately. A common misconception is that custom exceptions add unnecessary classes; instead they act as lightweight contract elements describing what can go wrong. Another trap is overuse: don't create an exception for every minor check. Prefer checked exceptions for recoverable conditions where callers should explicitly handle the situation, and prefer unchecked exceptions when the problem indicates a bug or misconfiguration. The core takeaway: custom exceptions improve readability and handling when used to model meaningful domain failures. Why create custom exceptions? means a custom exception is a user-defined class extending exception or runtimeexception to represent domain-specific failure.. In practical terms, express domain errors with precise types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing checked or unchecked for a custom exception is a design decision about who must do the work of recovery. Checked exceptions extend Exception and force callers to declare or catch them. Use checked exceptions when the caller can reasonably recover — for instance, an InvalidCredentialsException might be checked so calling code must handle prompting the user. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are used when the error indicates a programming mistake or unrecoverable configuration issue; callers are not forced to handle them. A common misconception is that checked exceptions are obsolete; rather, they are tools for A P I design when recoverability is expected. Another trap is overusing checked exceptions for every failure, which leads to noisy code. The practical rule from this chapter is simple: prefer checked for recoverable domain conditions, and prefer unchecked for developer errors or unexpected states. This distinction influences method signatures and how client code handles failure paths. Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions means use checked exceptions for recoverable domain conditions; use unchecked for programming or configuration errors.. In practical terms, how to choose between exception and runtimeexception. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the InsufficientFundsException and how BankAccount uses it. The exception stores required and available amounts so handlers can act on that data. In the constructor we call super(message) to preserve the exception message while keeping our fields for programmatic access. In BankAccount. withdraw we declare throws InsufficientFundsException, validate the input, and throw IllegalArgumentException for negative values. If balance is less than the requested amount we throw our custom checked exception with the message and numeric details. The calling code must catch InsufficientFundsException. In the example we catch it and print a structured error using getRequiredAmount and getAvailableBalance so the error handler can offer a retry or an alternate flow. A common misconception is to use strings alone for reporting; structured exceptions let you build UI decisions, logs, or retry logic based on numeric fields rather than parsing text. Practice: consider what additional context you might include in your own domain exceptions. InsufficientFundsException and BankAccount means a checked insufficientfundsexception carries numeric fields so callers can respond programmatically, not just print messages.. In practical terms, build a checked exception and see it used in code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Custom unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and are useful for configuration or programming errors that callers cannot reasonably handle. The chapter shows InvalidConfigurationException as an example: it signals missing application configuration and can optionally wrap a cause. Unlike checked exceptions, callers are not obliged to catch unchecked exceptions, which makes them appropriate for startup-time problems where there is no useful recovery path. In practice, reserve unchecked exceptions for situations where the program cannot continue or where handling would be scattered and unreliable. One misconception is to use unchecked exceptions purely to avoid changing method signatures; that hides the contract. If you expect callers to act, prefer checked. The example usage includes checking a system property and throwing InvalidConfigurationException when the property is absent and catches it only to report the configuration issue. This pattern keeps validation logic expressive while leaving runtime control flow clear. Using custom unchecked exceptions means invalidconfigurationexception models unrecoverable setup problems and can optionally include a cause to aid debugging.. try-with-resources replaces verbose finally blocks with a concise declaration that guarantees close is invoked. The pattern is simple: declare one or more resources that implement AutoCloseable in the try header. When the try block finishes, the runtime calls close() on each resource in reverse order of declaration. This behavior means resources are reliably released whether the try exits normally or by throwing an exception. A common mistake is assuming try-with-resources swallows exceptions; it does not. Exceptions from the try block still propagate to your catch, and any exceptions thrown during close are attached as suppressed exceptions to help debugging. Another trap is attempting to use types that do not implement AutoCloseable; the code will not compile. Benefits include less boilerplate, fewer null checks in finally blocks, and clearer intent. When you declare multiple resources in a single try-with-resources, Java closes them in reverse order. This is important when resources depend on each other, such as a FileReader wrapped by a BufferedReader. Closing the wrapper first prevents it from trying to use the underlying stream after it is closed. The code example declares FileReader first and BufferedReader second; on exit, BufferedReader. close runs before FileReader. close. This reverse closing order ensures nested wrappers are released safely. It also matters for suppressed exceptions: if the try block throws and a later close throws too, the close exceptions are suppressed and attached to the primary exception. A common mistake is assuming declaration order implies close order; it does not. Another practical benefit is that you can declare local resources that implement AutoCloseable inline in the try header, reducing the need for temporary variables and null checks in finally blocks. Suppressed exceptions occur when an exception thrown in the try block is followed by another exception thrown during automatic resource close. Java treats the first exception as primary and adds the later close-time exceptions to it as suppressed. This preserves the original failure context while making additional issues available via Throwable. getSuppressed(). A typical debugging approach is to log the primary exception and iterate over getSuppressed() to capture any secondary issues. There are predictable mistakes developers make when working with custom exceptions and try-with-resources. First, overusing custom exceptions for trivial checks clutters an A P I and creates maintenance overhead. Ask if a built-in exception already expresses the problem. Second, converting recoverable failures to unchecked exceptions hides the need for callers to handle foreseeable conditions. Third, failing to implement close() as idempotent can cause repeated cleanup logic to misbehave under multiple close calls. Fourth, not inspecting suppressed exceptions can hide important close-time failures; always check getSuppressed when debugging resource-related errors. Fifth, attempting to use try-with-resources with non-AutoCloseable types fails at compile time. Let's summarize the three core concepts to remember. First, a Custom Exception is a user-defined class extending Exception or RuntimeException to represent domain-specific errors. It carries structured details that enable programmatic handling and clearer logs. Second, try-with-resources is a Java 7+ statement that automatically closes AutoCloseable resources declared in the try header, reducing boilerplate and preventing resource leaks. Third, suppressed exceptions happen when a close() throws after a try-block exception; the primary exception is propagated and close-time exceptions are attached and retrievable via getSuppressed(), which is important for thorough debugging. Keep these concepts in mind: model failures at the appropriate level, use try-with-resources whenever possible, and inspect suppressed exceptions when cleanup problems occur.
